To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the virological effect of HAART is less pronounced in the CSF than in plasma, that the presence of resistance mutations in the cerebrospinal viral population does not predict the virological CSF response to HAART, and that the virologic CSF response to treatment may be independent of the plasma response.

the short-term virolelogical response to HAART in the CSF is lower than in plasma, that the CSF non/slow responder phenotype is frequent, and that the CSF virological response does not seem to be related to the presence of drug-resistant HIV-1 strains in CSF or plasma.

the short-term virolgic response of cerebrospinal fluids (CSF) to HAART was not predicted by baseline resistance mutations and that most CSF non/slow responder patients did not carry resistant HIV strains in CSF.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of antiretrovirals in the CNS, and the role that resistance mutations may play on the response of CSF to HAART.
the short-term virolgical response to HAART in the CSF of HIV-infected patients.
the effect of resistance on the virolelogical response of CSFs and the short-term effect of HAART on HIV replication in CSF.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a CSF VL decrease after HAART is not always observed in patients with a concomitant decrease in plasma VL.
the presence of resistance mutations in the cerebrospinal fluids of HIV-infected patients is not a good predictor of the short-term CSF virological response.
the CSF virological response is not predictable from the plasma response, and the presence of CSF-resistant virus does not appear to play a major role.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in patients treated with HAART, the presence of resistance mutations at the time of initiation of therapy is not a reliable predictor of the CSF virological response.
the CSF virological response in patients with neurological disease is not predictable on the basis of the presence or absence of genotypic resistant strains in the cerebrospinal fluids.
the CSF viral load is a marker of the central nervous system (CNS) infection, and the CSF response to therapy is an important marker of CNS response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CSF response to HAART is not always parallel with that observed in plasma.
the virological efficacy of antiretrovirals in the CSF is lower than in the plasma, and this is independent of the presence of resistant strains in the CSFs.

the presence of resistant strains in the cerebrospinal fluids (CSF) of patients with HIV-associated dementia is associated with an impaired CSF virological response, but not with the development of new resistance mutations.
